The Teachings and Spiritual Contribution of Rabbi Shimon Lavi: Leadership, Kabbalah, and Liturgical Poetry in the Post-Expulsion Era

This article surveys the life and considerable achievements of Rabbi Shimon Lavi, a multifaceted figure who served as a connecting link between the exiles of Spain and the community of Tripoli in Libya. The text focuses on Rashall's conscientious decision to abandon his lifelong aspiration to immigrate to the Land of Israel in favor of the spiritual and educational rehabilitation of Libyan Jewry, while leading halakhic reforms and serving as a physician in the royal court. The source analyzes in depth his two monumental works: the book Ketem Paz (Pure Gold), which constitutes an independent and unique kabbalistic commentary on the Sefer ha-Zohar (Book of Splendor), and the famous liturgical poem "Bar Yochai," which combines the mystical architecture of the ten sefirot with the biography of Rashbi. Finally, the article emphasizes Rashall's eternal legacy as one who saved an entire community from cultural annihilation and became its revered spiritual father unto this day.

The Teachings and Spiritual Contribution of Rabbi Shimon Lavi: Leadership, Kabbalah, and Liturgical Poetry in the Post-Expulsion Era

Biography and Milestones: From the Expulsion from Spain to Settlement in Tripoli

Rabbi Shimon ibn Lavi (Rashall) is numbered among the most fascinating and influential intellectual figures of North African Jewry in the sixteenth century.[1, 2] He was born in Castile, Spain, most likely in 1480 (5240) or 1485 (5245), and is thus considered the last of the kabbalists born on Spanish soil on the eve of the Great Expulsion.[3] His early childhood years were marked by the national trauma of the Expulsion from Spain in 1492, which forced his family to emigrate to the city of Fez in Morocco.[1, 3] In Fez, Rashall experienced exceptional spiritual and intellectual growth; he acquired a comprehensive Torah education in both exoteric and esoteric teachings, alongside extensive training in the sciences, astronomy (in which he was defined as an "expert"), and medicine, a profession in which he was certified and which served as a central tool in his later public activity.[3, 4, 5]

Historical research and communal documentation present two different versions regarding the circumstances of Rashall's arrival in Tripoli, Libya, and the precise dating of this journey:

Despite the chronological difference between the sources, there exists broad historical consensus regarding the decisive factor that led to his decision to end his journey in Tripoli and cancel his lifelong aspiration to immigrate to the Land of Israel.[4, 5] In the mid-sixteenth century, the Jewish community in Tripoli was in a state of deep spiritual and cultural decline, a result of severe persecutions, apostasy decrees, and frequent conquests by the Spanish and the Knights of the Order of Malta, which led to the implementation of Inquisition laws in the region.[1, 3, 5]

Communal historiography, as documented in the book Ma'aseh Tzaddikim (Acts of the Righteous) by Rabbi Avraham Khalfon, describes Rashall as one who was horrified to discover the dimensions of ignorance among the local Jews.[5] In his first encounters, he learned that on Friday nights most members of the community recited the Amidah prayer in the weekday version, and that the community lacked any halakhic leadership or Torah scholars.[5] From a profound sense of national responsibility, Rashall decided to sacrifice his personal longing for the Land of Israel, saying: "It is better for me to remain here and teach them Torah and commandments than to go to the Land of Israel."[5] He settled in the city, married there, and dedicated the next thirty-nine years of his life to the spiritual rehabilitation of the community.[4, 5]

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

The Spiritual Turning Point in Tripoli: Halakhic, Educational, and Public Rehabilitation

Rabbi Shimon Lavi is considered the spiritual reviver of Libyan Jewry and the one who reshaped its religious and legal identity.[3, 5] His activity encompassed all areas of communal life, while instilling the rich customs of Spain among the local community.[3, 5]

First, Rashall brought about a revolution in the education and teaching system.[4] He established batei midrash (study halls) that trained new generations of dayyanim (judges), Torah scholars, poets, and paytanim (liturgical poets), thereby creating the human infrastructure for the existence of a learned and independent community.[3, 4, 5]

Second, he reorganized the legal system by establishing orderly rabbinic courts.[5] These courts instituted social order and adjudicated according to Torah law in all matters of civil law—including neighbor disputes, loans, wills, gifts, negotiations, land sales, and contracts—alongside strict supervision of matters of religious prohibition and permission, betrothal, and divorce.[5]

In order to bridge the knowledge gaps of the common people, Rashall instituted practical liturgical regulations in the synagogues.[5] The most prominent of these was the regulation to recite the evening prayer aloud, a unique custom designed to enable the common people who were not proficient in reading to fulfill their prayer obligation by hearing the prayer leader.[5]

Alongside his spiritual roles, Rashall filled a high-ranking political and public position.[5] His extensive medical education enabled him to serve as the personal physician of Yahya Pasha, the governor of Tripoli on behalf of the Ottoman Empire.[2, 5] This status accorded Rashall enormous esteem from government officials and Muslim leadership, and he exploited this influence to protect the rights of the local Jews and prevent harm to the community.[4, 5] Because of this life's work, Rashall was compared by his contemporaries and subsequent generations to "Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai in the generation of the Destruction," as one who saved an entire community from spiritual and cultural annihilation.[5]

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

His Kabbalistic Doctrine and Scientific Thought: The Book Ketem Paz

The central intellectual work of Rabbi Shimon Lavi is the book Ketem Paz—an extensive and systematic commentary on the Sefer ha-Zohar on the Book of Genesis, which was written between 1561 and 1571 in Tripoli.[3, 6]

Re-canonization of the Jewish Library

In Ketem Paz, Rashall presents a revolutionary pedagogical and hermeneutic conception concerning the study hierarchy.[3] He granted the Sefer ha-Zohar, the Talmud, and the Bible equal canonical status, and even went so far as to determine in his composition that knowledge of esoteric teaching and the Zohar should precede the study of the Talmud.[3, 6] This conception was designed to provide both the common people and the educated alike with a spiritual anchor based on the inner dimension of Torah, as part of a process of rehabilitating national identity after the physical and spiritual crisis of the Expulsion.[3]

Intellectual Independence and Philosophical-Scientific Integration

The historical uniqueness of Ketem Paz in the study of Kabbalah derives from the fact that it represents a completely independent intellectual tradition, written shortly after the Expulsion from Spain without the influence of the kabbalistic study halls of Safed (the schools of Ramak and the Ari), which over the years became the accepted interpretation of the Zohar.[3, 6] Rashall developed and preserved the ancient Kabbalah of Gerona and Provence, while boldly integrating rationalist philosophical terminology under the influence of Rambam (Maimonides) and his book Moreh ha-Nevukhim (Guide of the Perplexed).[3, 6] He proposed a metaphorical interpretation of the parables found in the Zohar and saw its study as a sophisticated tool for meditation on the Divine.[6]

Additionally, his writings show the influence of his anonymous teacher from Fez, who apparently composed the "Commentary on Strange Words in the Sefer ha-Zohar"—a pioneering lexical work that Rashall used and even developed further.[3, 5] Rashall's writing method was characterized by techni
**Mystical Practice of "Mani'a Qolmusi"**

A mystical practice of "mani'a qolmusi" [automatic writing], defined as intuitive writing driven by higher spiritual inspiration.[3]

Another dimension of Rashal's mystical personality is reflected in his expertise in and belief in the doctrine of gilgul [reincarnation] and tiqqun [spiritual rectification].[5] Vivid testimony to this is found in the historical documentation recounting his encounter with a man of great stature who initially refused to come to him due to self-pride.[5] Rashal removed his tefillin, went to him personally, and urged him to reveal to him what his spiritual tiqqun was, while gazing at his face and identifying him as the gilgul of "Daniel the Beloved" [Daniel of the Book of Daniel].[5]

**History of the Book and Its Publication**

The name "Ketem Paz" was given to the composition by the Hida, who identified the precise gematriac connection between the book's title and the author's name, in addition to the word פ"ז being an acronym for "Perush Zohar" [Commentary on the Zohar].[3, 5] This connection is represented in the following equation:

Gematriya of "Ketem Paz" ≡ Gematriya of "Shimon Lavi"

The composition was preserved in manuscript for more than two hundred years in Tunis in the possession of Yeshua Tanji, and was first printed in Livorno in 1795 (5555) in two volumes by the press of Eliezer Sadon, at the initiative of the notable Yeshua Hakohen Tanuji and under the editorship of Rabbi Isaac Kalfon.[3, 5] Today, the book is considered an iron-clad asset in the world of Kabbalah; modern mequbbalim [kabbalists] make extensive use of it, and it constitutes a central source in the commentary "Matoq Midevash" of Rabbi Daniel Frisch.[3] Modern editions of the book have been produced by Rabbi Menahem Mekuvar, Rabbi Tal Haimowitz, and Rabbi Ronen Zer, with the assistance of the "Or Shalom" association of Libyan immigrants.[7]

**The Piyyut "Bar Yohai": Sefirotic Architecture and Talmudic Connections**

Rabbi Shimon Lavi is the author of the monumental piyyut "Bar Yohai" and also of its original melody.[1, 8, 9] The piyyut has become one of the most sacred and widespread liturgical texts in all Jewish communities, and it is studied and sung every Shabbat, festival, and appointed time, and especially on Lag Ba'Omer at the tomb of Rabbi Shimon bar Yohai (Rashbi) in Meron.[9, 10]

The piyyut is distinguished by a unique acrostic structure that immortalizes the name of the author "Shimon Lavi."[9] Beginning with the second stanza, immediately after the opening of the line with the words "Bar Yohai," a letter from Rashal's name appears according to the chronological order of his name.[9]

From a conceptual perspective, the piyyut is constructed as a magnificent synthesis that maps the historical and talmudic life story of Rashbi onto the theosophical structure of the ten sefirot, in ascending order from the lower sefirah of Malkhut to the uppermost sefirah of Keter [9, 11, 12]:

Malkhut (the first stanza - "Nimshahta ashrecha"): represents the reception of the supernal spiritual abundance defined as "shemen sasson" [oil of gladness].[11, 12]

Yesod (the second stanza - "Shemen mishhat qodesh"): identifies Rashbi with the attribute of the tsaddiq who channels holiness to the world.[11, 13]

Hod (the third stanza - "Moshav tov yashavta"): connects in practice the act of flight and concealment in the cave for twelve years from the Roman decrees, during which he acquired his mystical glory and splendor.[9, 11, 14]

Netsah (the fourth stanza - "Atsei shittim omedim"): describes Rashbi's disciples standing as "acacia trees" and studying the Torah of eternity and the light of the hidden flame.[9, 11, 14]

Tif'eret (the fifth stanza - "Velisadeh tapuhim alita"): Rashbi's ascent to the level of "haql tapuhin qaddishin" [the field of holy apples], where he united with the balancing Tif'eret, to the point that it was said of him "na'aseh adam ne'emar be'avurcha" [let us make man was said on your account].[11, 14]

Gevurah (the sixth stanza - "Ne'ezarta bigevurah"): reflects Rashbi's heroic and uncompromising struggle against Roman rule, his polemical silence, and his going out to spiritual war ("esh dat" [fiery law]) against the oppressors.[9, 11, 14]

Hesed (the seventh stanza - "Limqom avnei shayish higata"): Rashbi's arrival at the source of the pure white waters of Hesed, represented by pure marble stones and the face of a lion.[11, 14]

Binah (the eighth stanza - "Beqodesh haqodashim qav yaroq"): binding the channels of abundance of the sefirah of Binah, represented by the gate of the nun ("the secret of fifty") and the great jubilee.[11, 14]

Hokhmah (the ninth stanza - "Yod hokhmah qedumah"): gazing into the depths of the initial contribution of the thirty-two paths that characterize the divine Wisdom.[11, 14]

Keter (the tenth stanza - "Or mufla rom ma'alah"): reaching the summit of Keter, the wondrous light and the Ein Sof hidden from the eye of all living ("ta'alumah ve'ein qore lah" [concealment with none to proclaim it]).[11, 14]

**The Liturgy and Dissemination of "Bar Yohai" in the Jewish Diaspora**

Rabbi Shimon Lavi's piyyut has achieved unprecedented status in the Jewish liturgical canon, as many communities have incorporated it regularly into their prayer orders and customs, each according to its unique way [9]:

From a musical perspective, the piyyut has been granted an enormous variety of musical traditions.[9] The most widespread Middle Eastern melody originates in the region of Greater Syria, and it is incorporated in the order of baqashot singing of the Aleppo and Jerusalem communities, based on maqam saba (although the quarter tones were omitted in the popular Ashkenazic version).[9]

In parallel, rich and complex Hasidic melodies have developed, including the melodies of Ropshitz-Dzikov Hasidism, the joyful melody of Karlin Hasidism, the melodies of Boyan and Vizhnitz Hasidism, and also the monumental melody of Bobov Hasidism composed by Rabbi Ben Zion Halberstam of Krakow in 1920 (5680).[9] In recent years, a modern rhythmic melody from the repertoire of the singer Moshe Levi has also become very widespread.[9, 10]

**Additional Works and His Legacy for Generations**

Rabbi Shimon Lavi left an indelible mark also through additional compositions intended to regulate communal religious and customary life.[5]

He composed and corrected the "Seder Tiqqunei Kallah Leleil Shavu'ot" [Order of the Bride's Rectifications for the Night of Shavuot] according to the custom of the Jews of Tripoli, which was first printed in Venice in 1680 (440).[5] The tiqqun is built in a distinctly kabbalistic structure and divided into seven different orders, corresponding to the seven lower sefirot—from Hesed to Malkhut—with the purpose of connecting the holiness of the festival with the process of divine effluence.[5]

Rashal's legacy has remained a fundamental cornerstone in the identity of Libyan Jewry throughout the generations [5]:

Spiritual and familial continuity: His son, Rabbi Yosef Lavi, continued to function as a dayyan [rabbinical judge] and leader in Tripoli until his death in 1626 (386).[5] His grandson, Rabbi Shimon Lavi, continued in his path and first printed in Venice in the year 448 the famous prayer mahzor "Siftei Rennanot," which became the canonical prayer siddur of Libyan Jews.[5] Later descendants led the community, including Rabbi Yehudah Lavi and Consul Saul Lavi, who acted decisively and brought to a successful conclusion a severe blood libel that occurred in Libya.[5]

Perpetuation of his name among community members: As a token of appreciation and veneration for his life's work, most Tripolitanian Jews customarily named their sons "Lavi" in his memory, a tradition that was preserved through generations.[15]

Pilgrimage to his grave: His grave in Tripoli ("al-Dhahra") became a pilgrimage site for Jews and Muslims alike.[3, 5] In times of drought, cessation of rains, or public decrees, community members would ascend en masse to recite Psalms and pray at his grave, and communal tradition relates salvations and blessed rains that descended immediately after the prayers at the site.[5]

Rabbi Shimon Lavi represents in his personality the model of a leader who combines broad scientific, philosophical, and medical erudition together with uncompromising halakhic and mystical depth.[5, 6] His choice to forgo his aspiration to ascend to the Land of Israel for the sake of rebuilding Libyan Jewry transformed him into the spiritual father of the community and the one who shaped its character for generations.[4, 5]
